text.title: Inbound Intake Qualification Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules with rationale + source for inbound-intake-qualification. Includes terminal skip-this-methodology rule.

rule.statement: Every inbound lead MUST be scored against 5 questions: budget defined, decider identified, timeline within 6 months, scope describable in one sentence, fit with offering. Each scored 0 / 1 / 2.
rule.rationale: Without a fixed question set the consultant scores each lead against whatever that lead happened to emphasise, so a talkative prospect with no budget outranks a terse one with a signed budget line. Five fixed axes make leads comparable week to week. The 0/1/2 band is what keeps "budget was hinted at" from being recorded as "budget confirmed", which a yes/no field cannot express.

rule.statement: Score 8-10 → discovery call within 48h. Score 5-7 → async clarifying questions. Score 0-4 → reject with templated decline.
rule.rationale: A score with no pre-declared cut-off gets rationalised after the fact: in a slow month the consultant talks himself into a discovery call for a 4, and the rubric becomes decoration. Fixing the bands before the lead arrives removes that negotiation with yourself. The 48h window matters because a strong inbound lead is usually contacting several vendors at once and engages whoever answers while the problem still hurts.

rule.statement: Every reject MUST go via a templated decline that offers (a) why fit is unclear, (b) a recommended alternative resource. Silent ghosting forbidden.
rule.rationale: A ghosted lead is not a neutral outcome. It becomes a negative word-of-mouth data point inside exactly the network the inbound arrived from, and it forecloses the same buyer returning later with a budget that clears the floor. Declines get skipped when each one has to be composed from scratch, so the template exists to make the polite exit cheaper than silence.

rule.statement: If decider is unknown, qualifying call collects the decider's name + access path; refusal to share decider is auto-reject.
rule.rationale: A contact without signing authority can consume the entire discovery cycle and still not be able to say yes, after which the proposal has to be re-pitched to someone who never heard the problem framing and reacts to the price in isolation. Refusal to name the decider is itself the diagnostic signal: the contact is usually collecting a price benchmark or free advice on someone else's behalf.

rule.statement: If stated or implied budget is below your minimum, the lead is auto-rejected — you do not negotiate below the floor.
rule.rationale: Below-floor engagements do not consume proportionally less delivery attention, so the discount comes out of margin rather than out of scope. The exception is also not private: a discounted client refers others anchored on the price it paid, so after the first crossing the floor stops functioning as a floor and starts functioning as an opening position.

rule.statement: The rubric is reviewed quarterly against close-rate data; questions that don't predict conversion are dropped or replaced.
rule.rationale: The five questions encode a hypothesis about which signals predict a closed deal, and that hypothesis ages as the offering and the inbound channel change. An untuned rubric keeps confidently rejecting a segment that started converting two quarters ago, and nothing in day-to-day operation surfaces the error, because a rejected lead never returns to prove its score wrong. Only comparing scores against actual close rates closes that loop.

rule.statement: Every qualification decision is logged with the score + final outcome; the log feeds the quarterly tuning.
rule.rationale: Tuning needs the rejects, not just the wins. If only converted leads are recorded, a question that systematically screens out good business leaves no trace whatsoever, because the false negative is invisible by construction. Logging the score alongside the eventual outcome is the only mechanism that makes those misses countable at review time.

rule.statement: If inbound volume is below 1/month or all leads come from one referral channel, return `skipped`.
rule.rationale: A rubric pays for itself through volume and variance. Below one lead a month the scoring overhead exceeds the judgement it replaces, and the decision log never accumulates enough rows to tune against, so the quarterly review has nothing to work with. A single referral channel is the same problem from the other side: the referrer has already applied the filter, and the rubric only re-derives it.
